groups.text: It is currently 20 degrees and mostly clear in Berlin-Tempelhof.
With the morning weather set, here is the news.

Indian entrepreneur Bhavin Turakhia is betting thirty million dollars of his own money to challenge the dominance of Microsoft Office and Google Apps. His new venture, Neo, is an enterprise work platform that integrates documents, file storage, and project management into a single product. Turakhia believes workplace software designed before the AI era cannot simply be upgraded with chatbots. Instead, he argues these tools must be redesigned from the ground up to make artificial intelligence an active participant in daily work. By bootstrapping the project, Turakhia aims to avoid the structural disadvantages faced by incumbents who add generative AI to legacy products. Neo is built to be model-agnostic, which allows businesses to switch between different AI providers rather than remaining tied to one single source. This move marks Turakhia's fifth major venture in enterprise software over the last two decades.

The European Union's top court rules today on Google's appeal against a record antitrust fine of over four billion euros. This case stems from a 2018 penalty where the European Commission accused Google of abusing its Android market dominance by requiring phone makers to pre-install Chrome and Google Search. While the EU's General Court upheld those findings in 2022, it slightly reduced the fine. Google argues the sanction is unfounded and penalizes innovation, claiming users can freely download rival apps. The company has also accused the EU of ignoring similar practices by Apple on iPhones. In other news from Germany, a fire broke out early Thursday in the roof structure of the Helene von Bülow Clinic in Ludwigslust. Regional authorities report that two patients died and more than 30 people were injured. The blaze prompted a mass evacuation of the town's only hospital and disrupted local traffic.

June brought record-breaking temperatures across France, Spain, Great Britain, the Netherlands, Switzerland, and Germany. The German Weather Service reports that Germany has never experienced such intense heat this early in the year for such a long period. Environmental physician Claudia Traidl-Hoffmann warns that while humans can adapt to heat, the current intensity is simply too much for us. These heatwaves, featuring days above 30 degrees Celsius and nights staying above 20 degrees, place an enormous strain on the human body. This risk is highest for young children, pregnant women, the elderly, and those with pre-existing conditions. It also threatens people who perform heavy physical labor or work outdoors. Traidl-Hoffmann notes that while bodies exposed to heat continuously are better trained for it, true adaptation to changing environmental conditions requires time that we may not have.

Tensions are rising within Germany's coalition committee as the CDU, CSU, and SPD debate a new package of reforms. A central point of contention is whether to loosen protections against dismissal. The Berliner Tagesspiegel suggests that while some in the Union would prefer to abolish these protections entirely, the left wing of the SPD views such moves as an attack on employees. The paper argues that changes are overdue, specifically suggesting that protections be eased for high earners in the six-figure range rather than eroding them for the general workforce. However, the Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung warns that this debate sends a signal of insecurity to a nervous public. This friction comes at a time when industrial job losses are mounting, with up to 100,000 positions potentially at risk at Volkswagen and uncertainty growing over how artificial intelligence will reshape the labor market.

Evaluating the originality of visual images has long been a challenge for creativity assessment, but new research suggests multimodal large language models can now act as judges. In a study by William Orwig and Roger E. Beaty, six models—including Gemini 3 Flash, Gemma 4 31B IT, GPT-5.4 Mini, GLM-5v Turbo, Kimi K2.5, and Qwen 3.6 Plus—were tested on their ability to score visual creativity without any prior fine-tuning or human examples. The models evaluated 992 AI-generated images and 1,500 hand-drawn sketches, showing substantial alignment with human ratings. While automated scoring has already proven effective for verbal tasks, this research explores whether the step-by-step reasoning provided by these models offers an interpretable window into how they actually arrive at their creativity scores. This shift toward zero-shot visual evaluation moves AI beyond simple image recognition and into the more subjective territory of artistic judgment.

Russian forces launched a major drone and missile attack on Kyiv overnight, killing at least 13 people. Ukrainian officials say children were among a significant number of casualties as strikes rocked buildings across several neighborhoods. Tymur Tkachenko, head of Kyiv's military administration, stated that Russia deliberately targeted residential areas, while the Russian Ministry of Defence claimed it targeted energy facilities. In Birmingham, West Midlands Police are investigating a shooting on Bowyer Road in Alum Rock. A 16-year-old boy was taken to the hospital with potentially life-threatening gunshot injuries; police noted the incident happened near a mosque but do not believe the two are connected. Shifting to sport, British singles players at Wimbledon are fighting to lift the gloom after all ten home players lost their first-round matches on Monday. Four Britons, including Katie Swan, secured wins on Tuesday and play their second-round matches this Thursday.

A woman groomed by a predatory Met Police officer says that despite receiving a substantial payout, she regrets reporting him. She describes her nine-year battle to be believed as more horrendous than the abuse itself, while the Met has apologized for how its Professional Standards unit compounded her distress. In Leicestershire, a BBC investigation found Twana Jamal, a convicted people smuggler once called the godfather of French migrant camps, living and working illegally under a false name. Law enforcement officials in mainland Europe say fifteen other convicted smugglers are likely in the UK, raising questions about border controls. Meanwhile, in Australia, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese clashed with Opposition Leader Angus Taylor over a recent speech. The exchange followed a question from MP Ben Small regarding Joseph Dowd, who spent over 33,000 dollars on billboards and an auction item to criticize tax changes.
After the headlines, back to the weather.
This afternoon will be partly cloudy with no rain expected and temperatures between 22 and 27 degrees.
And from the weather, a quick look at the calendar.

On your calendar today: Your personal calendar has household maintenance all day, ChatGPT MxM at four thirty in the morning, and Greifen at seven in the evening. Your work calendar has Open Office at one in the afternoon, a meeting with Aaron at two, an AutoML Seminar at four, and the Summer Bash at six.
And that's it for your personal morning broadcast.
[mature adult voice, intensely emotional, tender, radiant; hold a long breath after Rise] Rise... and shine.
[very very long pause before speaking; then mature adult voice, most emotional, strong, warm, radiant, deeply encouraging; hold a long breath after Rise] Rise... and shine.
